data.name: MegaSphere
data.detailed_description:
Play as a special ops combat unit sent to investigate why the stars around Solar System are going dark in MegaSphere — a story-based post-cyberpunk action platformer adventure game of supermassive scale set in early 22nd century: smart guns, robots, self-reconstructing environments, and vast AIs.

RANDOMIZE EVERYTHING
New world each time you play

TOUGH ENEMIES
Those AI's are called 'intelligence' for a reason

UPGRADEABLE WEAPONS
A homing flamethrower, a wall-destroying graviton, a bouncing RPG?

THE SCI-FI LOOK YOU'VE LOVED
Pixel art + pixel-perfect modern lighting engine

PERMADEATH WITH CHECKPOINTS
One life per user, unless you're a cat

PHYSICS-BASED PLATFORMING
Believable, alive world. So good it hurts

GAMEPAD OR MOUSE+KEYBOARD
Designed to work with your favorite control scheme

reviews.review:
There are a lot of technical gameplay issues that need addressing, like pacing and enemy scaling. 

Early on in the game you have weapons that simply do not do much damage against enemies that have a relatively large amount of health and hit hard enough to take a full bar of health within a hit or two (purple bullet enemies.) This makes it a game that would be ideal for some sort of shield, evade, or deflect mechanic, yet none exists. You can't even hide behind cover, since the terrain is incredibly destructible by most enemies.

While just about everything about the game is beautiful, it suffers from the identity crisis issue of not throwing itself entirely into one genre or the other. In one sense it has some Dark Soulsian difficulty, a 'bonfire' mechanic (manually activated in-world checkpoints,) and a world that only vaguely tells you sometimes where you should be going. That clashes with the seeming randomization of the game, where enemy placement is mixed up and unpredictable, meaning that the aforementioned problem of not being able to effectively deal with enemies is absurd. At least in Dark Souls you could roll away. The dash in this game is virtually worthless, (it amounts to the body length of ATAI, the main character,) since it covers almost no distance.

If you shoot at something long enough, it does eventually die, but there are so many random enemies everywhere that I have no idea what most of them do until I've either died or lost 90% of my health. It bears repeating, since it is obvious the devs are taking concepts from it, that Dark Souls used pacing very efficiently in the enemy types one faced at various stages of the game. This game doesn't. 

I've seen laser cannons, missile launchers, incendiary automatic weapons, and basically everything else on the enemies and I barely played an hour and a half. In most games of this genre, you see smaller, weaker enemies with less dangerous weapons to star. Sure, I'm fine with them doing a bar of health, but when I'm fighting something that can chase me into a corner with all the health in the world, fire almost continuously, and chunk my health with bullets that never end, that's a problem. That's a mid-late game situation in most games of this genre. They do that right. This game... you have every enemy and weapon combination attacking you from the start, but you have access to a peashooter with a couple superficial (read: worthless) upgrades like bounce, penetration, and multiply. Those don't help me kill anything faster, they just let me cheese certain enemies by abusing line of sight and aggro. Not really emergent gameplay.
